1000005.etyen:

en.g: a male given name from Middle Norwegian [in turn from Old Norse, in turn from Latin, in turn from Ancient Greek], equivalent to English Andrew
a surname transferred from the given name, derived from the male given name Anders

1001285.etyen:
Inherited from Middle Norwegian Anders, a medieval vernacular form of Andreas (“Andrew”), formed through metathesis of Andres. The name ultimately derives from Latin Andreas, from Ancient Greek Ἀνδρέας (Andréas, “Andrew”), associated with ἀνδρεῖος (andreîos, “manly”), from ἀνήρ (anḗr, “man, human being”). In Norway, the name is first attested in the 14th century.
Doublet of Andreas (“male given name”), Andres (“male given name”), and André (“male given name”).
Compare Norwegian Nynorsk Anders, Danish Anders, Swedish Anders, Finnish Anders, Icelandic Anders, English Andrew, German Andreas, Fren

1001541.etyen: From Old Norse sérligr. Cf. Norwegian Nynorsk særleg and Danish særlig. Related to Swedish särskilt. The Swedish and Danish word is never used as an interjection.

a-class weak verb; a weak verb characterized by an -a (“-a”) ending in the preterite and supine, especially the Nynorsk conjugation class which has -ar (“-ar”) in the present and -a (“-a”) in the preterite and supine
x: «Kaste» er et a-verb på nynorsk: «kastar – kasta – har kasta».
“Kaste” is an a-class verb in Nynorsk: “kastar – kasta – har kasta”.
Det riksmålsforkjemperne gjør, er å ta bort a-verba fra bokmål.
What the Riksmål advocates are doing is removing the a-verbs from Bokmål.

1004101.etyen:
Compound of a (“the letter a; an a-ending”) + verb (“verb”), literally “a-verb”.
The first element refers to the characteristic -a (“-a ending”). The second element, verb (“verb”), is borrowed from Latin verbum (“word; verb”), from Proto-Italic *werðom (“word”), from Proto-Indo-European *werdʰom (“word”), ultimately from the root *werh₁- (“to speak, say”).
Compare Norwegian Nynorsk a-verb (“a-verb”).

1004613.etyen:
From Mons (“male given name”) + -sen (“patronymic suffix meaning “son of””), preserving adjacent ⟨ss⟩ at the morpheme boundary, originally a patronymic meaning “son of Mons”. The given name Mons is a traditional Norwegian form of Magnus.
Compare Danish Monsen and Swedish Månsson (“patronymic surname”).

1005125.etyen:
PIE word
 *h₂éd
Compound of e-moll (“E minor”) + akkord (“chord”), literally “E-minor chord”.
The first element e-moll (“E minor”) contains the musical note name e (“E”) and moll (“minor”). The latter is via German Moll (“minor”) from Middle High German bēmolle (“B-flat; soft B”), from Medieval Latin b molle (“soft B”). The adjective is from Latin mollis (“soft, mild”), from Proto-Italic *moldus (“soft”), from Proto-Indo-European *ml̥dús (“soft, weak”), from the root *(s)meld- (“to soften, melt”).
